title: Given a string s and a list of words all of the same length, find all starting indices in s of substrings that are a concatenation of every word exactly once in any order. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 4: Words Concatenation (Substring with Concatenation of All Words)
keyPoints: All words have the same fixed length L, so any valid concatenation is exactly L * wordCount characters long.
The window slides in whole-word steps of length L, not character by character.
Run the window once for each of the L possible starting offsets to cover all word boundary alignments.
Build a requirement map of word frequencies; maintain a seen map of words inside the window.
When a word exceeds its required count, shrink from the left until it is back within quota.
If an unknown word is encountered, clear the window and restart past it.
Time is O(|s| * L) because each of the L offsets does a linear scan with O(L) per word comparison.

s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window in whole-word steps, tracking word counts against the requirement, and record each start where every word appears exactly the required number of times.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Words concatenation** – finds every start index where a substring consists of all given words concatenated exactly once in any order.
- **Fixed word length** – all words share the same length L, so valid substrings are exactly L * wordCount long.
- **Per-offset scanning** – the window runs once for each offset 0 to L-1, because word boundaries only align on multiples of L from a given start.
- **Word-level window** – the window adds and removes whole words of length L, maintaining a seen-count map against a requirement map.
- **Complexity** – O(|s| * L) time, O(wordCount * L) space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, settlement messages contain fixed-length three-character instruction codes laid end to end. A complete settlement batch requires a specific multiset of codes. Rajesh scans the message stepping three characters at a time and records every position where a run of consecutive codes forms a complete batch.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Words Concatenation: s = "BARFOOTHEFOOBARMAN"
words = ["FOO", "BAR"], L = 3, wordCount = 2, totalLen = 6

  Offset 0: boundaries at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ right=0: "BAR" valid, seen{BAR:1}, m=1  │
  │ right=3: "FOO" valid, seen{FOO:1}, m=2  │
  │ m==2 -> record left=0, remove "BAR"     │
  │ right=6: "THE" unknown, clear, left=9   │
  │ right=9: "FOO" valid, seen{FOO:1}, m=1  │
  │ right=12:"BAR" valid, seen{BAR:1}, m=2  │
  │ m==2 -> record left=9, remove "FOO"     │
  │ right=15:"MAN" unknown, clear           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Result from offset 0: [0, 9]

  Offsets 1 and 2: no additional matches

  Final result: [0, 9]

  Window at offset 0:

  B A R F O O T H E F O O B A R M A N
  └──┬──┘└──┬──┘
    BAR     FOO  -> matched! record 0
                └──┬──┘
                  THE  -> unknown, reset
                        └──┬──┘└──┬──┘
                          FOO    BAR -> matched! record 9
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Words Concatenation asks for every start index where a substring is the concatenation of all given words exactly once in any order. Because all words share the same fixed length L, any valid substring is exactly L times the word count characters long and consists of back-to-back L-length chunks. You think in terms of words, not characters.

The key structural insight is that word boundaries from a given start only land on multiples of L from that start. To cover all possible alignments, you run the window once for each offset from 0 to L-1. For each offset, the right boundary advances one word at a time, extracting each chunk. If a chunk is not a required word, you clear the window and restart past it. If it is required, you add it to a seen map and shrink from the left while it exceeds its quota.

The per-offset decomposition is what keeps the total work bounded at O(|s| * L). Each character participates in at most a constant number of word extractions across all offsets, and the window operations (clear, add, remove) each cost O(L) for the substring extraction. Precomputing word-to-integer identifiers can reduce the comparison cost for long words.

At the National Bank of India, the settlement gateway processed long instruction messages made of fixed-length codes. A complete settlement batch required a specific multiset of codes, and the system located every position where such a batch began. The per-offset word-level window found all batch starts in a single pass proportional to the message length.

Remember one sentence: run a word-level sliding window once for each of the L possible offsets, and record every position where the seen word counts match the requirement.
